tip: Body states use estar com plus a noun: estou com calor is literally 'I'm with heat'. Spanish reaches for tengo, French for j'ai, but Portuguese picks estar com.
tenho muito sono is literally 'I have much sleep'. Portuguese uses ter, to have, where English uses 'to be' for this state.
cozinha does double duty: it is both 'she cooks', the verb, and 'the kitchen', the noun. Context tells you which.
The circumflex marks number: têm is the eles/elas form, while tem is the ele/ela form. Eles têm três filhos needs the accent.
estar covers how you are right now: está ocupado means busy at the moment, not that he is a busy sort of person.
todo before a singular noun means 'every': todo dia is 'every day', todo mês is 'every month'.
estou com saudade is how you say you miss someone: saudade, like fome or frio, takes estar com, not a direct verb.
gostar always needs de before its object: gosta de cozinhar. English 'like' takes no preposition, but dropping de here breaks the sentence.
vocês is the everyday 'you all' across Brazil; the older tu forms survive only in some regions.
Use estar, not ser, for where someone is right now: está no escritório places him at the office at this moment.
trazer is to bring toward you, here: posso trazer um amigo. Use levar instead for taking something away from where you are.
quero um café is perfectly polite in Portuguese; add por favor and it carries none of the bluntness English 'I want' would.
estar plus an -ndo verb marks an action in progress: está trabalhando is 'she is working' right now.
No helper word like English 'do' for questions: Você trabalha keeps plain statement order and rising intonation makes it a question.
casa meaning 'home' drops the article: para casa is 'homeward'. Add one and a casa becomes a specific house.
gostar always takes de: gostamos de caminhar. English 'like' has no preposition, but drop de here and the sentence breaks.
fica means 'is located': onde fica o restaurante. Brazilians reach for ficar, not estar, for where a place sits.
ir plus an infinitive is the everyday future: vou fazer compras means 'I'm going to shop'. It beats the simple future in speech.
Do not mix up vir, to come, as in podem vir, with ver, to see. One letter apart, two different verbs.
Buildings and landmarks take ser for location: o hotel é perto da praia. Location is not automatically estar.
Onde tem uses tem for 'there is/are' where textbooks write há: Onde tem um restaurante is 'where is there a restaurant'.
dos is de plus os fused into one word: o mais velho dos irmãos means 'the oldest of the brothers'.
Marital status takes ser, not estar: sou casado. Portuguese treats it as who you are, not a passing condition.
estou com fome is literally 'I'm with hunger': body states use estar com plus a noun, not a direct adjective.
num is em plus um squeezed together: num apartamento means 'in an apartment'.
estar marks a state happening right now: está ocupada agora says she is busy at this moment, not by nature.
aproveitamos o feriado uses aproveitar, 'make the most of'. On its own, aproveita is Brazil's everyday way to say 'enjoy'.
Yes/no questions keep statement word order: Vocês usam o metrô stays put and rising intonation alone turns it into a question.
ir plus an infinitive is the spoken future: vai começar means 'he is going to start'. It outpaces the simple future in speech.
estar plus an -ndo verb makes the present continuous: estou aprendendo is 'I'm learning', an action underway right now.
Inherent traits take ser: a água do mar é salgada. Salt is part of what seawater is, not a passing state.
For where a place is, Brazilians use ficar: Onde fica o banheiro means 'where is the bathroom', with ficar marking a settled location.
dar aulas, literally 'to give classes', means to teach: dou aulas de português is 'I teach Portuguese'.
estar plus a gerund is English '-ing' in progress: estamos planejando means 'we are planning'. Brazilians lean on it constantly.
Portuguese asks Qual é, not O que, for numbers and names: Qual é o seu número. It is 'which is' where English says 'what'.
In speech Brazilians use tem for 'there is': tem uma farmácia means 'there's a pharmacy'. The textbook há sounds formal.
ao is the preposition a fused with o: vamos ao cinema means 'we go to the cinema'.
dar certo is literally 'to give right' and means to work out: vai dar certo says 'it is going to work out'.
ser for identity, estar for the moment: é advogada says what she is, está trabalhando what she is doing right now.
ligar takes para, not a direct object: you call to someone in Portuguese. ligou para você is 'called you'.
para points toward a goal or destination, por toward a reason or exchange: para a viagem is 'for the trip', aimed at it.
Nouns ending in -ção are always feminine: a recepção, a estação, a informação. That is why it is na recepção.
mapa is masculine despite the -a ending: o mapa. Greek-rooted -ma nouns do this too, like o problema and o sistema.
ficar marks a fixed location, more settled than estar: a estação fica a dois quarteirões, 'the station is two blocks away'.
Ask a name with Qual é, not O que: Qual é o seu nome. Portuguese uses 'which is' where English reaches for 'what'.
estar plus a gerund is the right-now '-ing': está lendo means 'you are reading'. Brazilians use it more than the simple present.
